##

:::: {.r-fit-text .absolute top="300"}

Where does authority come from in language?

::::

::: {.notes}
Many of you, in observation notes, still want to call some kinds of language "bad grammar" and other kinds of language "good grammar".

:::

## Authority depends on context

::: {.incremental}

- One of the biggest problems with **prescriptivism** is the way it ignores the social and affective meanings of language
- When we use a word, we are not only attempting to share its **denotation** with the listener
- We also choose words for their **connotations**
- And we choose words, and sounds, and syntactic structures, etc. that are **appropriate to the social situation**

:::

## Authority depends on context (cont.)

- What counts as "good" or "bad" language has to depend on:
    - who is saying it?
    - who is listening?
    - where are you?
    - what are you trying to accomplish?

## Gen Z is the authority on Gen Z slang

- Each generation rejects anything older people said that still *seems* age coded:
  - Millenials: the pause, adulting, stan, lit, mood, salty, I can has
  - Gen X: hella, clutch, wack, bogus, fly, fresh, janky, radical
  - Boomers: groovy, far out, square, righteous, drag, fuzz (meaning police)
- Each generation also tends to reject anything people younger than them say that *seems* age coded:
  - Gen Alpha: skibidi, brain rot, rizzler, sigma, mog?, glaze?

## But slang is an important way that words enter the lexicon

- awful, banter, belch, bellhop, bender (drinking), bet (wager), bomb (fail), bootcamp, bootleg, booze, bouncer, brunch, bubble, bully, bungee, cheesy, chum, clobber, clueless, cool, cop, cuss, ditch (v), **divvy**, dreamy, **exam**, fake, fan, flick, flog, fluke, flunk, frat, gal, gawky, geek, grouchy, growler (beer bottle), **gym**, hack (cope), hairy (difficult) heist, hellacious, **hello**, hit (kill), hunch, jay walking, jinx, job, jock, joystick, kid, lag (v), meme, misfit, mob, **ok**, OJ, pal, patrol, pec (muscle), pinpoint, poke, **pub**, rave, scram, sender, sham, shenanigan, shuffling, slang, stoner, super, suss out, swag, teenager, varsity, wimp, wonky, etc.

## Mental Lexicon

![](images/Skull_and_brain_normal_human.svg.png){.absolute right="0" width="30%" bottom="0"}

- All of this information about words is stored in our **mental lexicon**
  - Structured by pronunciation & meaning (both)
  - Includes:
    - lexical category
    - how it works in a sentence
    - pronunciation
    - meaning(s) (denotation, affect, social)
  - Words in our mind are linked to other related words

# How does context matter?



* Scenario: Dinner table conversation
  * Q1 – Is there a state income tax in Connecticut?
    * R1 – Yes\, No\, or I don’t know
    * Simply informational
  * Q2 – Is there any salt on the table?
    * R2 – Yes\, No\, I don’t know…or passing the salt\!
    * Not meant to be information request
    * First three responses are rude\!


![](images/8-Is%20slang%20legit_1.png)


---


![](images/8-Is%20slang%20legit_2.jpg)

# Pragmatics



* __Pragmatics __ is the study of language use\, in particular\, the relationship among syntax\, semantics\, and interpretation in light of the  _context of the discourse_
  * Discourse = sequence of language\, joined in situation
  * Context = where we are\, what came before\, etc\.
  * Differs from  __semantics __ in that the focus there is on meanings of words\, sentences\, and phrases  _in isolation_  _\, without regard to contextual information_

---


# Media

[https://www\.youtube\.com/watch?v=MPwpk\-YgvjQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MPwpk-YgvjQ) stop at 5:29


---


# Q slide

True or false: Relevance is one of the four main assumptions that pragmatists talk about when it comes to communication\. True


---




* We say that native speakers have two things:
  * __Grammatical competence__  – the ability to produce and assign meaning to grammatical sentences
    * Our unconscious\, or implicit\, knowledge of vocabulary\, pronunciation\, sentence structure\, and meaning\.
    * Everything a native speaker says = grammatical
  * _AND_
  * __Communicative competence __ – the ability to produce and interpret utterances relevant to their context of use
    * Our ability to use language  __appropriately__  in each context to achieve the function that we intend to achieve
    * This is the part we’ll be focusing on here\!


# Patterns of use


---


![](images/8-Is%20slang%20legit_3.jpg)

# Contexts of use



* Let’s consider the example from the video:
* “Can you close the window?”
  * Interrogative sentence = a request for information \(that is\, “Are you able to close the window?”\)
  * But\, in a specific context\, say\, one where two people are trying to study in a room with an open window\, but the marching band is practicing on the field next door…
    * It serves as a request for action
    * The speaker wants the addressee to shut the window
    * Expected response ≠ “Yes”\, “No”\, “I don’t know”

---


# Real world contexts also call for…

![](images/8-Is%20slang%20legit_4.png)



* __Sociolinguistics __ is the study of the interaction of language and social factors
  * It’s a two\-way street – language influences society and society influences language\!
  * Language doesn’t exist in a vacuum
* Plus\,  _NO ONE speaks the same way ALL THE TIME_
  * They vary by age\, gender\, race\, situation\, region\, style\, etc\.
  * So…context matters\!

---


![](images/8-Is%20slang%20legit_5.jpg)

# Why do people vary their speech?



* People have at their disposal an entire  __linguistic repertoire__
  * The set of language varieties exhibited in the speaking and writing patterns of a speech community
  * We adjust to the speech situation = who\, what\, where\, when\, why\, how\, etc\.
  * Remember communicative competence\!
* Languages \(and dialects\, styles\, registers\, etc\.\) can differ in vocabulary\, phonology\, grammar\, semantics\, etc\. across a variety of speech situations
* We’ll focus on lexical and semantic markers of differences in speech situations
::: {.notes}

Purpose = The kind of activity taking place and the interlocutors’ goals guide language choice
Setting = Changes in topic, location, and mode of communication (speaking vs. writing) guide language choice
Participants = Identities of the speaker and addressee and their roles in the interaction guide language choice

:::


---


# Q slide

Name one language\-related thing that is \(potentially\) different between talking to someone at a funeral vs\. talking to that same person at a bar\.


---


# Lexical Markers


---


# Slang

![](images/8-Is%20slang%20legit_6.png)



* Contrary to popular belief\, slang ≠ bad speech
* __Slang __ is the register used in situations of  _extreme informality_
  * Its use may signal rebellious undertones or an intentional distancing of its users from certain mainstream values
  * But it may also signal cultural knowledge\, intimacy\, belonging
  * Everyone can use slang\, given the appropriate situation
* Slang ≠  __jargon__
::: {.notes}

Jargon is a specialized vocabulary associated with professions (such as medicine, finance, and engineering) and with activities (such as sports, music, and computing)
Unlike slang, jargon isn’t limited to situations of extreme informality and doesn’t carry rebellious undertones
Words often have meanings other than those in the profession/activity
Example
Baseball: plate, pitch, curveball, changeup, swing, hit, run, out, homerun, closer, reliever, doubled, singled, homered, etc.

:::


---

---


# But is slang legit?

![](images/8-Is%20slang%20legit_7.png)



* Our question for today was about legitimacy though
  * What makes any part of language “legit”?
* Some would say that a word is legit if it’s in the dictionary…
  * _Babygirl_
  * _Dudebro_
  * _Hot rodent man_
  * _Chemo brain_
